division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.38   Subject to rule 3.41, if a statement of claim includes a claim
for the recovery of property and one or more defendants do not file
a statement of defence or demand for notice, the plaintiff may enter
judgment against that defendant or those defendants for the
recovery of that property, and the plaintiff is entitled to a costs
award.

BOOK_B.title: Judgment for recovery of property

commentary.text: Rule 3.38 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.38. 1. When a Plaintiff Can Use R. 3.38 to “Recover” Property In TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R. 1, 56 Alta. L.R. (5th) 363, the Plaintiff sued the Defendant for breach of a contract under which the Defendant sold a hotel and its parking lot to the Plaintiff. The relevant facts were summarized in paragraph 1 of the decision: 1 TLA Food Services Ltd. (TLA) entered into a contract (the Contract) with 1144707 Alberta Ltd. (1144707) to purchase a hotel. Unknown to the Plaintiff and to its principal, Tilemachos Tziachris, the hotel and hotel parking lot were located on two parcels. The hotel building is located on both, and the hotel parking lot is situated entirely on one of them. The land description in the Contract did not include the parcel on which the parking lot and part of the building are located. TLA sued 1144707, who did not defend and was noted in default. Justice Shelley dismissed an application to rectify the contract, and then discussed whether the Plaintiff could recover the parking lot land pursuant to R. 3.38. She said, at paragraphs 45–52: 45 However, if I am wrong, and the Contract can be rectified, I will consider whether default judgment can be entered under Rule 3.38 to permit TLA to obtain title to Property 2. 46 Rule 3.38 provides that, when no defence or demand for notice is filed to a claim for recovery of property, the Plaintiff may enter judgment for the recovery of that property. The immediate predecessor of this Rule is R. 149. Neither Rule has been subject to judicial commentary or discussion. Stevenson and Cote, in both the 2009 and 2010 Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook, (Edmonton, Juriliber, 2009 and 2010), have no commentary regarding either version of the Rule. 47 Rule 3.38 adds a parenthetical comment “[When no defence is filed in a foreclosure action]”, which initially seems to suggest that the Rule is applicable only to foreclosure actions. However, that parenthetical comment follows the phrase “Subject to rule 3.41”. Rule 3.41 is entitled “When no defence is filed in a foreclosure action”, and provides that “If a defendant in a foreclosure action does not file a statement of defence or demand for notice, the plaintiff must note the defendant in default before filing an application …” This suggests that the parenthetical reference is to alert the reader to the nature of the “subject to”, rather than to indicate that the Rule applies only to foreclosure actions. On the plain language of the Rule itself, there is no indication that it is so limited. 48 Rule 3.38 provides for “recovery of property”. R. 149 provided for the “recovery of goods or land”. In the successor Rule 3.38 “property” includes both “land and personal property”: Rules of Court, Appendix: Definitions. The plain meaning of “recovery” is to take back something that the Plaintiff previously possessed—to get back or regain something. See Oxford English Dictionary (www.oed.com, July 19, 2011): 4a. The regaining or restoration to one's control or possession of a thing lost, stolen, or otherwise taken away, retrieval; the possibility of recovering such a thing. 49 “Recovery” also has a legal meaning, set out in the Oxford English Dictionary (www.oed.com, July 19, 2011) as: 2a. The fact or process of gaining or regaining possession of or a right to property, compensation, etc., by a legal process or judgment. 50 In my view, this definition is not applicable here. “Recovery” in the latter definition is a general term describing remedies broadly. In that sense, a plaintiff in every action is always seeking recovery for what he asserts he has lost; that recovery may be assessed as damages, specific performance, or some other order. In this context, I find that “recovery of property” references the restoration or regaining of property or title. 51 Moreover, the context of the Rules dealing with default judgment and noting in default further support this interpretation. Rules 3.37, 3.38 and 3.39 provide for two kinds of default judgment—a judgment on application to the Court after a defendant has been noted in default under Rule 3.36. Such a judgment requires an assessment under Rule 3.37. The second form of judgment does not require that a defendant first be noted in default (except in the case of foreclosure (Rule 3.41)) and does not require an application to the Court. These judgments are those for a debt or liquidated demand (Rule 3.39), or “recovery of property” (R. 3.38), and are entered by the plaintiff. 52 In the case of debt or liquidated demand, the jurisprudence has established that such default judgment is only when an exact or easily calculable amount is sued for. Logically, under the similar Rule 3.38, default judgment for the recovery of property should only be available when the property is easily ascertainable, without the need for a Court application. This would be the case in a foreclosure action, where the plaintiff has a mortgage identifying its interest, or in a bailment action, where the plaintiff has an agreement describing the personal property sued for.
